content: 1. The widespread implementation of mass vaccination programs since the 1960s has significantly curtailed the spread of diseases such as smallpox, polio, measles, and tetanus (Delany 2014; Whitney 2014). 2. In the late 1940s and 1950s, prior to the advent of public vaccination programs, poliovirus caused infantile paralysis with high mortality rates, affecting hundreds of thousands of children (Global Polio Eradication Initiative 2016; WHO 2016a). 3. The measles virus was responsible for post-infectious encephalomyelitis in approximately 1 in 1,000 infected individuals, often resulting in permanent central nervous system impairment (Miller 1964; CDC 2017). 4. Today, polio is nearly eradicated (WHO 2016a), and global deaths from measles have decreased by 79%, with an estimated 17.1 million deaths prevented between 2000 and 2014 (WHO 2016b). 5. The effectiveness of vaccinations has been repeatedly demonstrated since the introduction of the cowpox vaccine in the 18th century (Delany 2014; Whitney 2014). 6. Vaccination is widely regarded as one of the greatest achievements of modern medicine (Delany 2014; Whitney 2014). 7. The primary goal of vaccination is to prevent infectious diseases and to eradicate highly contagious and deadly viral diseases on a global scale (Delany 2014; Whitney 2014). 8. Current routine vaccination programs recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) include vaccines against tuberculosis (BCG), hepatitis, polio, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (DTP), Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal bacteria, rotavirus, measles, mumps, rubella, and human papillomavirus (HPV) (WHO 2017). 9. Additional vaccination programs are proposed for specific regions, high-risk populations, and pathogens with unique characteristics, such as Bacillus anthracis, which causes anthrax. 10. One of the most recent additions to mass vaccination programs is the HPV vaccination program, launched in the USA in 2006 (WHO 2014). 11. HPV is a causative agent of cervical cancer, the second most common cancer in women, and the HPV vaccine aims to prevent this disease (WHO 2014). 12. Over 60 countries have incorporated the HPV vaccine into their routine vaccination schedules following its market approval (Bruni 2016). 13. HPV vaccines have been evaluated for efficacy (immunogenicity) in clinical trials and were approved based on their ability to elicit a strong immune response against HPV or to prevent persistent HPV infections (Harper 2017). 14. However, the duration of protection provided by HPV vaccination, as well as its long-term effectiveness in reducing cervical cancer incidence, remains to be conclusively demonstrated (Kjaer 2018). 15. Early results indicate benefits of HPV vaccination in reducing cervical pathology among vaccinated individuals (Harper 2017; Kjaer 2018). 16. Concerns have been raised regarding adverse events potentially associated with HPV vaccines. 17. Between 2006 and 2012, following the approval of Gardasil® in the USA, 21,265 adverse events were reported to the national Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) (Tomljenovic 2012). 18. HPV vaccines have been linked to a higher number of reported adverse events compared to other vaccines (Tomljenovic 2012). 19. In the European Union, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) received similar reports but found no scientific evidence of a causal association (EMA 2015). 20. Several observational studies also failed to identify associations between HPV vaccination and clinical diagnoses (Klein 2012; Arnheim-Dahlström 2013; Donegan 2013; Grimaldi-Bensouda 2014; Scheller 2015), though some researchers have challenged these findings (Brinth 2015a; Brinth 2015b; Dyer 2015; Gøtzsche 2016a; Gøtzsche 2016b). 21. Symptoms reported following HPV vaccination include headache, orthostatic intolerance, fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, blurred vision, bloating, abdominal pain, light sensitivity, and involuntary muscle activity (Brinth 2015a; Brinth 2015b). 22. Despite the consistency of reported symptoms, they do not align with a well-defined disease category or diagnosis but instead present as a constellation of nonspecific symptoms (Brinth 2015a; Brinth 2015b). 23. Observational studies relying on registered diagnoses may have excluded a significant proportion of eligible participants with unclear adverse symptoms. 24. Most young girls reporting adverse events following HPV vaccination do not receive a clinical diagnosis and are therefore unlikely to appear in medical registries. 25. Randomized clinical trials on HPV vaccines, which formed the basis for safety assessments, have been criticized for not using true placebos (e.g., placebos without any vaccine or adjuvants) as the control intervention (Exley 2011). 26. Furthermore, HPV vaccine trials offered vaccination to control groups after the scheduled follow-up period, precluding meaningful long-term comparisons between vaccinated and control groups (FUTURE II Study Group 2007; Paavonen 2009). 27. Vaccination mimics infection in the body and triggers the activation of a robust immune response (Coffman 2010; Kool 2012; O’Hagan 2012; Oleszycka 2014). 28. The purpose of vaccination is to induce long-lasting protection against a specific pathogen while minimizing unwanted adverse effects. 29. Vaccines can be categorized into two types: traditional vaccines containing antigens and excipients (substances formulated alongside the active ingredient) without adjuvants, and newer-generation vaccines that typically require the addition of adjuvants (Coffman 2010; O’Hagan 2012). 30. Vaccine antigens may consist of whole attenuated pathogens, pathogen components, virus-like particles, or genetic material from the pathogen (Strugnell 2011). 31. Like other medicinal products, vaccines undergo preclinical testing for safety, carcinogenic risk, immune response induction, and overall efficacy before being licensed and marketed. 32. Rare or delayed-onset adverse events are not easily detected during the relatively short duration of most preclinical and clinical studies. 33. Post-marketing safety surveillance in the general population is essential, as demonstrated over the years (Ward 2000; Chen 2006). 34. For example, the childhood measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, introduced in the late 1960s, was a mixture of three live attenuated viruses administered via injection (Offit 2007). 35. Over time, safety concerns arose regarding the MMR vaccine, with reports of serious fever seizures, meningitis, and allergic reactions among vaccinated individuals (Kimura 1996; Dourado 2000; Ward 2000).
